summary: For ages 5–7: children learn that WILD, FARM and PET are categories about an animal's RELATIONSHIP WITH PEOPLE, not fixed labels stamped on a species. Wild animals find their own food and shelter in nature; farm animals are kept by people for food, wool, milk or eggs; pets are kept for companionship. The central insight is that the SAME kind of animal (e.g. a rabbit) can be wild, farmed OR a pet depending on how it lives with people — so children reason 'how does it live / why is it kept?' rather than memorising a label. Children also learn the safety rule: wild animals are watched from a distance — look, don't touch or feed.
misconceptions: Believing an animal's category is fixed by its species — not realising the SAME kind of animal can be wild, farmed or a pet depending on how it lives with people.
Thinking 'wild' means dangerous/fierce (so a wild rabbit or wild duck doesn't count as wild), rather than 'lives independently in nature'.
Assuming all farm animals are pets because they're friendly/kept by people, blurring 'kept for food/produce' with 'kept for companionship'.
Thinking wild animals in parks or gardens are tame and safe to approach or feed — missing the observe-from-a-distance safety point.
Calling any animal seen at a zoo or petting farm a 'pet', confusing where an animal is kept with the reason it is kept.

activities.title: Sort the animals into Wild, Farm and Pet
steps: Set out three baskets or labelled areas: WILD, FARM, PET (on paper, as cut-out pictures, or on a drag-and-drop screen with three bins).

Sort clear examples and say WHY aloud as each one is placed: fox and lion → WILD ('the fox finds its own food'); cow and sheep → FARM ('the sheep gives us wool'); goldfish and hamster → PET ('the hamster is for company').
Apply a one-line test to each animal as you sort: wild = looks after itself in nature; farm = kept to give us food/wool/milk/eggs; pet = kept for company.
When an animal lands in WILD, say the safety reminder: 'watch wild animals from a distance — look, don't touch or feed.'
activities.insight: Each category can be checked with a simple one-line rule about how the animal lives and why people keep it — not by how big, fierce or cute the animal looks.

activities.title: The same animal, three ways
steps: Look at (or draw) the SAME animal in three situations: a rabbit hopping free in a hedgerow, a rabbit in a hutch on a farm kept for meat/fur, and a rabbit curled up as a child's pet.
Decide which is wild, which is farmed and which is a pet, and explain how you can tell them apart.

Place each of the three rabbit pictures into a basket from Activity 1 and discuss why rabbits, as a kind of animal, can go in WILD, FARM or PET. Each rabbit goes in only one basket, depending on how that rabbit lives with people.

Repeat with other 'it depends' animals: a cat (pet vs feral/living wild), a hen (farm hen kept for eggs vs a pet hen kept for company), a pig (farm pig vs feral pigs living wild in some places; wild boar are their wild relatives).
activities.insight: The category is not a property of the species; it describes the animal's relationship with people, so the same kind of animal can belong to more than one group depending on how it lives.

activities.title: Talk and check: why do we keep this animal?
steps: Answer short 'why' questions out loud or in a quick check: 'Who gives the pet rabbit its food? Who feeds the wild one?', 'Could one cat be a pet while another cat lives wild — how?', 'Is a cow wild, a farm animal, or a pet — and why?'
Answer a safety question: 'Why should we watch a wild animal from far away instead of picking it up?'
Optionally take on a farmer or vet role and explain to someone else why a particular animal is kept (for food/wool/eggs, or for company).
activities.insight: Children can state one clear difference for each group and justify a category by the animal's relationship with people, including the safety reason for keeping distance from wild animals.

checkQuestion: A rabbit hopping about in a field, and a rabbit in a hutch in someone's garden. Are they the same kind of animal? Which one is wild and which is a pet — and how can you tell?
checkAnswer: They are the same kind of animal (both rabbits). The field rabbit is wild — it finds its own food and shelter and has no owner; the hutch rabbit is a pet — a person feeds it and cares for it for company. You tell them apart by how the animal lives and its relationship with people, not by what kind of animal it is.
